title: "5. Robustness over splits"
output: github_document
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 3.8, dpi = 150)
```

```{r load}
source("R/plotting.R")
sp <- readRDS("results/splits.rds")
J <- length(sp)
f4 <- function(v) sprintf("%.4f", v)
f3 <- function(v) sprintf("%.3f", v)
```

The results of parts 2 to 4 come from one split of the clients into training
and test sets. Here the whole procedure is repeated on `r J` new splits: a new
stratified test set of 25%, new folds, the features, the tuning of both models
by cross-validation on the training part (20 boosting configurations instead
of 30, to keep the run time reasonable), the final fit and the evaluation on the
test part. The numbers come from `scripts/run_splits.R`.

The test sets of different splits overlap, so the `r J` results are not
independent and their spread understates the uncertainty. Intervals on this
page use the corrected resampled $t$ statistic of Nadeau and Bengio (2003),
which inflates the variance of the mean difference $\bar d$ over $J$ splits to

$$
\left( \frac{1}{J} + \frac{n_{\text{test}}}{n_{\text{train}}} \right) s_d^2 ,
$$

where $s_d^2$ is the sample variance of the differences across splits.

```{r helpers}
nb_interval <- function(d, ratio = 1 / 3) {
  se <- sqrt((1 / length(d) + ratio) * var(d))
  q <- qt(0.975, length(d) - 1)
  c(mean = mean(d), lo = mean(d) - q * se, hi = mean(d) + q * se)
}
S <- simplify2array(lapply(sp, `[[`, "scores"))   # model x metric x split
```

## Predictive performance

```{r scores}
lab <- c(constant = "Constant", rule = "Rule PAY_1 >= 2",
         logit_raw = "Logistic, raw", logit_engineered = "Logistic, engineered",
         xgb_raw = "XGBoost, raw", xgb_engineered = "XGBoost, engineered")
ms <- function(v, f) sprintf("%s (%s to %s)", f(mean(v)), f(min(v)), f(max(v)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  model = lab,
  `test log loss, mean (min to max)` = sapply(names(lab), function(m) ms(S[m, "log_loss", ], f4)),
  `test AUC, mean (min to max)` = sapply(names(lab), function(m) ms(S[m, "auc", ], f3)),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr")
```

```{r comparisons}
comp <- list(
  c("logit_engineered", "logit_raw"),
  c("xgb_engineered", "xgb_raw"),
  c("xgb_engineered", "logit_engineered"),
  c("logit_engineered", "rule")
)
ct <- t(sapply(comp, function(cc) {
  d <- S[cc[1], "log_loss", ] - S[cc[2], "log_loss", ]
  c(nb_interval(d), wins = sum(d < 0))
}))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  comparison = sapply(comp, function(cc) paste(lab[cc[1]], "vs", lab[cc[2]])),
  `mean difference in log loss` = sprintf("%+.4f", ct[, "mean"]),
  `95% interval` = sprintf("[%+.4f, %+.4f]", ct[, "lo"], ct[, "hi"]),
  `splits where the first is better` = sprintf("%d of %d", ct[, "wins"], J),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrr")
```

The conclusions of parts 2 and 3 hold across splits, and every interval in the
table excludes zero. The engineered features improve the logistic regression by about `r f3(-ct[1, "mean"])` in log loss and
boosting by about `r f3(-ct[2, "mean"])`, and boosting beats the logistic
regression on the engineered features by about `r f3(-ct[3, "mean"])`. The
boosting gain from the engineered features is the smallest effect on the page
and the only one that reverses on a split (`r J - ct[2, "wins"]` of `r J`).

## Simulated value

```{r value}
r_grid <- sp[[1]]$r_grid
V <- simplify2array(lapply(sp, `[[`, "value"))   # r x policy x split
D <- V[, "xgb", ] - V[, "logit", ]                 # r x split
low <- r_grid < 0.15
mid <- r_grid > 0.2 & r_grid < 0.6
reg <- rbind(
  low = nb_interval(colMeans(D[low, , drop = FALSE])),
  mid = nb_interval(colMeans(D[mid, , drop = FALSE]))
)
wins <- c(low = sum(colMeans(D[low, , drop = FALSE]) > 0), mid = sum(colMeans(D[mid, , drop = FALSE]) > 0))
pts <- function(v) sprintf("%+.1f", 100 * v)
```

Part 4 found that XGBoost is worth more than the logistic regression when
acting is cheap ($r < 0.15$) and slightly less in the middle of the range
($0.2 < r < 0.6$), with regions drawn after looking at the test set. The same
regions, now fixed in advance, give on the new splits:

| region | XGBoost minus logistic, mean | 95% interval | splits where XGBoost is ahead |
|---|---|---|---|
| $r < 0.15$ | `r pts(reg["low", "mean"])` points | [`r pts(reg["low", "lo"])`, `r pts(reg["low", "hi"])`] | `r wins["low"]` of `r J` |
| $0.2 < r < 0.6$ | `r pts(reg["mid", "mean"])` points | [`r pts(reg["mid", "lo"])`, `r pts(reg["mid", "hi"])`] | `r wins["mid"]` of `r J` |

```{r value-plot, fig.height = 3.8}
dl <- data.frame(r = rep(r_grid, J), diff = as.vector(D), split = rep(seq_len(J), each = length(r_grid)))
dm <- data.frame(r = r_grid, diff = rowMeans(D))
ggplot(dl, aes(r, diff)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.2, xmax = 0.6, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(aes(group = split), colour = palette_main["light"], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = dm, colour = palette_main["dark"], linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_axis) +
  labs(title = "XGBoost minus logistic regression, simulated value captured",
       subtitle = paste0("Thin lines: ", J, " splits; thick line: mean; shaded: middle region"),
       x = "Cost ratio r (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_report()
```

```{r verdict, include = FALSE}
low_holds <- reg["low", "lo"] > 0
mid_holds <- reg["mid", "hi"] < 0
```

`r if (low_holds) "The advantage of XGBoost at low cost ratios is confirmed: it holds on average across splits with an interval that excludes zero." else "The advantage of XGBoost at low cost ratios is not confirmed with confidence: the interval across splits includes zero."`
`r if (mid_holds) "In the middle range the logistic regression is again ahead, and the interval excludes zero." else paste0("In the middle range the lead of the logistic regression found in part 4 does not survive: no statistically detectable difference in simulated value was found between the two models in this region. This is not a proof of equivalence, which would need a margin fixed in advance, but the interval rules out differences larger than about ", sprintf('%.1f', 100 * max(abs(reg['mid', c('lo', 'hi')]))), " points.")`
`r if (!mid_holds) "Part 4 was a single test set, and this is the kind of result that a second look is for." else ""`

## What this changes

```{r summary-numbers}
xl <- ct[3, ]
```

The ranking by predictive quality is stable: engineered features over raw ones,
boosting over the logistic regression, and both far ahead of the rule. The
economic comparison is more fragile, which is expected, since it depends only on
the clients near one threshold rather than on all of them. The conclusion that
survives is the one stated as a business choice in part 4: at low cost ratios
boosting is the better candidate, and in the middle of the range no difference
in simulated value between the two models could be detected.

## Scope of this check

The ten splits reuse the same 30,000 clients, including those of the original
test set, and the two cost regions were defined after the analysis of part 4.
This is a check of how stable the results are to the choice of split, not a
validation on new data. That would require clients from another period or
another bank, which this data set does not contain.
